The Number Of Linux Games Has More Than Quadrupled In The Past Two Years

Okay, I'll be the guy who dares post the unpopular. First off, before you downvoat and go on the attack, know this: I use Linux and have since the mid-90s. I'm not attacking Linux!

That said, there are zero signs that people are moving to Linux for gaming. Linux usage on Steam remains below 1%. And when you take into account that Valve launched a fairly well known initiative to entice people over (with Steam Machines and SteamOS) there is no real reason to believe that Linux will ever rival Windows as the PC gaming platform of choice. Steam Machines and SteamOS are utter failures. They haven't sold well and they haven't brought over any measurable new users.

Now that said, I think it's great that there are more games available for Linux. It certainly is good for people who live on Linux. It's just not correct to assume that Linux will be a real challenger to Windows in this market or even put a dent in that platform. Vulkan seems like it will help make more games accessible to Linux users, but don't hold your breath for the platform to be embraced by the larger gaming community.

That said, there are zero signs that people are moving to Linux for gaming.

En masse, perhaps not, but even just the boards here suggest people are moving to Linux for gaming. And frankly, a mass exodus is not what we want or need -- it would cripple both the Linux gaming community, and the Linux community at large, as wave after wave of inexperienced users moved onto the platform. As far as Linux has come, it's still not the most newbie-friendly system in the world.

Steam Machines and SteamOS are utter failures.

I disagree. If you judge them based on units sold contrasted against, say, modern platform systems, then yes, they have had a terrible showing to date. But that's not the point; the point is to show that there is interest, and to provide an avenue by which developers can begin to deliver multiplatform products with at least some guaranteed user-base. And in that regard, Valve's efforts have been spectacularly successful, as illustrated by the explosion in the number of games available on Linux since they began their efforts. Even tangentially-related services like Wine are seeing development spikes the likes of which they've never seen in the history of the project, all because of Valve and its boasts.

Not unreasonable points, but not persuasive IMHO. You certainly can't take Voat's love of Linux as anything but confirmation bias. This place is full of anti-authoritarian, Windows-hating, Trump supporting, Linux users. Not knocking them, but anecdotal data isn't in any way supported by actual usage rates as published by Valve, nor is it reflected in other trend lines.

As to Steam Machines and SteamOS, I just flat out disagree since these are business ventures. Steam Machines, in particular, rely on hardware partners who will quit marketing and selling them if people don't buy them. We're already very close to that point--the only big-name company on board is Alienware, and I believe they already sell the same rig with Windows 10. If folks aren't buying the product, they'll drop the line. I bought an AndroidTV (Vizio) when they were released--same kind of dynamic. In many ways, a more open, feature-rich experience than Roku or AppleTV--few bought it and all the partners bailed. Also, the "specs" that Valve requires of Steam Machines are basically meaningless to gamers--I understand the concept. The goal was to make a rig that was like consoles in that you'd be guaranteed to run certain games. That dynamic is anathema to PC gaming and there's zero data to suggest that folks use that as a deciding factor in pre-built rigs where customization & upgradeability are key. I'm not convinced that Valve should be solely credited with the increase in Linux gaming, but you may be correct. They made a lot of noise about Steam Machines and Steam Boxes and they have a lot of clout in the industry--HOWEVER if they fail to deliver customers then it doesn't matter. Vulkan, on the other hand, should reduce the friction of porting, so I expect the number of games to keep going up. Again, although that's great for folks who use Linux, it is meaningless (as it pertains to business) if customers don't adopt the platform. In sum: Valve is a business and everything they do is oriented towards profit. Judge them as a business and not necessarily an ally of Linux. If they were successful in actually bringing gamers over to SteamOS/Linux, I'd give them credit. There are currently no signs that anything they have done has resulted in gamers switching to SteamOS (or even Linux). If such metrics existed folks could proclaim it was a worthwhile investment. As it stands, the only purpose it has served is as a hedge against Microsoft. It might have helped push MS to keep gaming on the PC "open" but beyond that, it's currently the 3DO of the new millennium.
